Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Claim Interpretation
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f):
(f) Element in Claim for a Combination. – An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph:
An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
The claims in this application are given their broadest reasonable interpretation using the plain meaning of the claim language in light of the specification as it would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.  The broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim element (also commonly referred to as a claim limitation) is limited by the description in the specification when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, is invoked.
As explained in MPEP § 2181, subsection I, claim limitations that meet the following three-prong test will be interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph:
(A)	the claim limitation uses the term “means” or “step” or a term used as a substitute for “means” that is a generic placeholder (also called a nonce term or a non-structural term having no specific structural meaning) for performing the claimed function;
(B)	the term “means” or “step” or the generic placeholder is modified by functional language, typically, but not always linked by the transition word “for” (e.g., “means for”) or another linking word or phrase, such as “configured to” or “so that”; and
(C)	the term “means” or “step” or the generic placeholder is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function.
Use of the word “means” (or “step”) in a claim with functional language creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is to be treated in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. The presumption that the claim limitation is interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, is rebutted when the claim limitation recites sufficient structure, material, or acts to entirely perform the recited function.
Absence of the word “means” (or “step”) in a claim creates a rebuttable presumption that the claim limitation is not to be treated in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. The presumption that the claim limitation is not interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, is rebutted when the claim limitation recites function without reciting sufficient structure, material or acts to entirely perform the recited function.
Claim limitations in this application that use the word “means” (or “step”) are being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, except as otherwise indicated in an Office action. Conversely, claim limitations in this application that do not use the word “means” (or “step”) are not being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, except as otherwise indicated in an Office action.
This application includes one or more claim limitations that do not use the word “means,” but are nonetheless being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, because the claim limitation(s) uses a generic placeholder that is coupled with functional language without reciting sufficient structure to perform the recited function and the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier.  Such claim limitation(s) is/are: “sample collection chamber connector configured to form a seal with an opening” in claim 1; “liquid capture interface … which captures at least one of chemical markers and biological markers from the breath sample” in claim 1; “air diverter … arranged to divide the sample delivery part into an upstream portion and a downstream portion” in claim 1; “a volumetric breath quantifier configured to measure a volume of breath” in claims 5-6; and “closure member configured to selectively close the sample outlet” in claim 7.
Because this/these claim limitation(s) is/are being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, it/they is/are being interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification as performing the claimed function, and equivalents thereof.
The sample collection chamber connector is defined as a push fit, screw fit or bayonet attachment (page 8 lines 31-34); the liquid capture interface is defined as a salt solution (e.g. a phosphate buffered salt solution), a culture medium (e.g. a tryptic soy broth) or water for injection (page 10 lines 9-13); the air diverter is defined as a wall (page 13 line 28); the volumetric breath quantifier is defined as one or more rotatably mounted blades or sails (page 15 lines 29-33); and the closure member is defined as a binary valve (page 16 lines 4-6 and line 18).
If applicant does not intend to have this/these limitation(s) interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, applicant may:  (1) amend the claim limitation(s) to avoid it/them being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph (e.g., by reciting sufficient structure to perform the claimed function); or (2) present a sufficient showing that the claim limitation(s) recite(s) sufficient structure to perform the claimed function so as to avoid it/them being interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION. —The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 1-11 and 13-21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Claim 1 recites the limitation the breath from the patient in lines 25-26.  There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim. The limitation should recite the breath sample from the patient.
Claims 2-11 and 13-21 are rejected by virtue of depending from rejection claim 1.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis (i.e., changing from AIA  to pre-AIA ) for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
Claims 1-4, 10-11, and 14 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Dr Moschos (US 20210093226 A1) in view of Pan (US 20040077093 A1), further in view of Sherwood et al. (US 20180110444 A1) (herein Sherwood).

Annotated figures 1A and 11 of Dr Moschos
Regarding claim 1, Dr Moschos discloses a breath sampler for collecting a breath sample from a patient, the breath sampler (figure 13, paragraphs [0001, 0086], an exhaled breath condensate collection device; mouthpiece module 100 and collection vessel housing 200) comprising: a non-rebreather part (figure 13, paragraph [0086], mouthpiece module 100) comprising: a sample inlet (figure 1, paragraph [0074], a mouthpiece breath inlet port 122 and mouthpiece breath inlet tube 132); an outlet arranged to allow air to exit the non-rebreather part (figure 1a, mouthpiece breath outlet tube 134) the outlet and the sample inlet defining a first portion of an internal breath flow pathway therebetween (figure 1a, paragraph [0074], mouthpiece first chamber 130; mouthpiece breath inlet tube 132 and mouthpiece breath outlet tube 134 providing a breath passageway from within the mouthpiece first chamber 130); and a sample delivery part in fluid communication with the non-rebreather part at an upstream end via the outlet (annotated figure 1a,  paragraph [0090], collection vessel has a vessel breath inlet (326) for admitting exhaled breath into the chamber; and in fluid communication with the mouthpiece breath outlet port (124))), the sample delivery part defining a second portion of the internal breath flow pathway (annotated figure 1A, second chamber), the sample delivery part (annotated figure 1A, paragraphs [0074, 0090], second chamber having mouthpiece breath outlet port 124 in fluid communication with vessel breath inlet 326, and mouthpiece exhaust tube 138) comprising: a sample outlet in the upstream portion (figure 1a, paragraphs [0074, 0082], mouthpiece breath outlet tube 134 and mouthpiece breath outlet port 124; vessel breath tube 330); a return inlet in the downstream portion and in fluid communication with an exhaust (figure 4, paragraphs [0074, 0077, 0082, 0087], mouthpiece exhaust inlet port 136; a mouthpiece exhaust outlet port 140 at a downstream end; vessel exhaust tube 332; and mouthpiece exhaust 164 through which exhaled breath can exit the device); and a sample collection chamber connector (paragraphs [0086], recess connection members 170) configured to form a seal with an opening of a sample collection chamber (figures 10 and 13-14, paragraphs [0086-0087], collection vessel housing 200 is typically attached to the mouthpiece module 100 whilst the mouthpiece is in the sealed configuration; lip 324 acts to withdraw the sliding lid 322 whereby to expose the sealing film (not shown) covering the openings of the vessel breath inlet 326 and the vessel exhaust outlet 328), the connector defining a perimeter (annotated figure 11, paragraph [0086], recess connection members 170 having a perimeter), the sample outlet and the return inlet being disposed within the perimeter (annotated figure 11, paragraphs [0085- 0086], recess connection members 170 having a perimeter having mouthpiece exhaust inlet port 136 and mouthpiece breath outlet port 124), wherein the breath sampler further comprises the sample collection chamber coupled to the sample collection chamber connector (figure 14, paragraphs [0086-0087], collection vessel housing 200 is mounted to the mouthpiece module 100; collection vessel 300 is inserted into the collection vessel housing 200 through the collection vessel receiving opening 206), wherein the breath sampler is configured so that, during operation, the breath from the patient passes through the non-rebreather part (paragraph [0074], first chamber 130; mouthpiece breath inlet port 122 configured to receive exhaled breath from a subject and a mouthpiece breath outlet port 124 arranged to be in fluid communication with the mouthpiece breath inlet port 122 to form a breath passageway and to output exhaled breath out of the mouthpiece module 100), is delivered via the sample delivery part to the sample outlet into the sample collection chamber (paragraph [0090], fluid conduction from a mouthpiece breath inlet port (122) for receiving exhaled breath to a mouthpiece breath outlet port (124); and collection vessel (300) defines a sealed and resealable chamber for collecting exhaled breath condensate in use; having breath inlet (326) for admitting exhaled breath into the chamber, the breath then re-enters the sample delivery part from the sample collection chamber via the return inlet, and escapes the breath sampler via the exhaust (paragraphs [0077, 0082, 0085], mouthpiece exhaust 164 through which exhaled breath can exit the device; a vessel exhaust outlet 328; a breath passageway from the mouthpiece 162 to the mouthpiece housing breath outlet port 166 and from the mouthpiece housing exhaust inlet port 168 to the mouthpiece exhaust 164). Dr. Moschos further discloses a dividing member 128 divides the mouthpiece inner component 120 and defines a boundary of the mouthpiece first chamber 130 (and second chamber) (paragraph [0074]). Dr Moschos does not disclose a one-way outlet valve; an air inlet arranged to be closed by a one-way inlet valve arranged to allow air to enter the non-rebreather part, the air inlet being in fluid communication with the first portion of the internal breath flow pathway; an air diverter, in the sample delivery part, arranged to divide the sample delivery part into an upstream portion and a downstream portion; the sample collection chamber comprising a liquid capture interface; and wherein the breath sampler is configured so that, during operation, the breath from the patient passes through the liquid capture interface in the sample collection chamber, which captures at least one of chemical markers and biological markers from the breath sample.
In a similar technical field, Pan discloses a one-way outlet valve arranged to allow air to exit the non-rebreather part (figure 2, paragraph [0063],  check valve 123 disposed in the collection branch 109 permits the breath sample to flow through the branch and into the container 117); an air inlet arranged to be closed by a one-way inlet valve arranged to allow air to enter the non-rebreather part, the air inlet being in fluid communication with the first portion of the internal breath flow pathway (figure 2, paragraph [0063], check valve 115 permits air to be taken in through the intake end 113, but does not permit the subject's breath to pass out through the intake end); the sample collection chamber comprising a liquid capture interface(paragraph [0065], the container 117 of the detection unit 105 is constructed for holding a volume of liquid L; diffusion of the breath sample by the head 125 facilitates retention of any ammonia in the sample by the liquid L); and wherein the breath sampler is configured so that, during operation, the breath from the patient passes through the liquid capture interface in the sample collection chamber, which captures at least one of chemical markers and biological markers from the breath sample (paragraph [0065], the container 117 of the detection unit 105 is constructed for holding a volume of liquid L; diffusion of the breath sample by the head 125 facilitates retention of any ammonia in the sample by the liquid L).
In a similar technical field, Sherwood discloses an air diverter, in the sample delivery part, arranged to divide the sample delivery part into an upstream portion and a downstream portion (paragraph [0086], gas sampling device 1010 has a diverter valve 1050 (or other component) that is configured to selectively route exhaled air to the exhaust port 1054 and the gas testing chamber 1026).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Dr Moschos such that the breath sampler further comprises a one-way outlet valve arranged to allow air to exit the non-rebreather part; an air inlet  arranged to be closed by a one-way inlet valve arranged to allow air to enter the non-rebreather part, the air inlet  being in fluid communication with the first portion of the internal breath flow pathway; an air diverter, in the sample delivery part, arranged to divide the sample delivery part into an upstream portion and a downstream portion; the sample collection chamber comprising a liquid capture interface; and wherein the breath sampler is configured so that, during operation, the breath from the patient passes through the liquid capture interface in the sample collection chamber, which captures at least one of chemical markers and biological markers from the breath sample as disclosed by Pan as such a modification would have been predictable, namely incorporating the check valve 115 of Pan into the mouthpiece breath inlet tube 132 of Dr Moschos to permit air to be taken in through the intake end, but does not permit the subject's breath to pass out through the intake end (Pan, paragraph [0063]), incorporating the check valves 123 of Pan into the mouthpiece breath outlet port 124 of Dr Moschos such that that the orientation of the check valve 123 is reversed to permit the breath sample to flow outwardly from the mouthpiece end through the tube, sample collection branch, container and vent, and to block air flow through the vent, sample collection branch, container and tube toward the mouthpiece end (Pan, paragraph [0064]), substituting the wall of Dr Moschos for the diverter valve of Sherwood to selectively route air (Sherwood, paragraph [0086]) and incorporating the liquid L of Pan into the collection vessel 300 of Dr Moschos to  facilitate the retention of any ammonia in the sample by the liquid L (Pan, paragraph [0065]). Further upon the modification of Dr Moschos to incorporate the liquid L of pan into the collection vessel 300 of Dr Moschos, Dr Moschos further discloses wherein the breath sampler is configured so that, during operation, the breath from the patient passes through the non-rebreather part, is delivered via the sample delivery part to the sample outlet into the sample collection chamber, passes through the liquid capture interface in the sample collection chambers which captures at least one of chemical markers and biological markers from the breath sample, the breath then re-enters the sample delivery part from the sample collection chamber via the return inlet, and escapes the breath sampler via the exhaust.
Regarding claim 2, upon the modification of Dr Moschos to incorporate the liquid of Pan into the collection vessel 300, as described with respect to claim 1 above, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 1, further comprising a sample delivery tube coupled to the sample outlet for delivering the breath sample to the liquid capture interface (paragraph [0074], mouthpiece breath inlet port 122 and mouthpiece breath outlet tube 134 providing a breath passageway from within the mouthpiece first chamber 130 to the mouthpiece breath outlet port 124), and wherein the sample delivery tube is removably connected to the sample outlet (figure 2b, paragraph [0075], second inner component 123 is removable from the first inner component 121 of the mouthpiece inner component 120 for cleaning of the saliva trap formed therein).
Regarding claim 3, Dr Moschos discloses the breath sampler according to claim 2 and a vessel breath tube 330 which extends within the phial 302 (paragraph [0082]). Dr Moschos does not disclose a diffuser coupled to the sample delivery tube, the diffuser comprising an inlet and a network of channels to divide the breath sample from the inlet into a plurality of streams.
In a similar technical field, Pan discloses a diffuser coupled to the sample delivery tube (paragraph [0065], sample connection branch 109 which includes a diffuser head 125 is immersed in the liquid), the diffuser comprising an inlet (sample connection branch 109 including diffuser head 125) and a network of channels to divide the breath sample from the inlet into a plurality of streams (paragraph [0065], small openings 126 in the diffuser head 125; diffusion of the breath sample by the head 125 facilitates retention of any ammonia in the sample by the liquid L).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Dr Moschos such that the breath sampler further comprises a diffuser coupled to the sample delivery tube, the diffuser comprising an inlet and a network of channels to divide the breath sample from the inlet into a plurality of streams as disclosed by Pan, as such a modification would have been predictable, namely incorporating the diffuser head 125 having small openings 126 of Pan onto the vessel breath tube 330 of Dr Moschos such that the head 125 facilitates retention of any ammonia in the sample by the liquid L (Pan, paragraph [0065]).
Regarding claim 4, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to 1, wherein the air diverter comprises a wall extending in a plane that is transverse to the longitudinal axis of the sample delivery part (figure 2b, annotated figure 1A, paragraph [0074], dividing member 128 divides the mouthpiece inner component 120 and defines a boundary of the mouthpiece first chamber 130 and second chamber).
Regarding claim 10, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 1, further comprising a plurality of selectively connectable modules (figures 2b and 6, paragraphs [0075, 0078], first inner component 121 further comprises two connection members 125 arranged to slidably engage with corresponding connection members 127 provided on the second inner component 123; connecting protrusion 202 on each side of the collection vessel housing 200 into the two recess connection members 170).
Regarding claim 11, upon the modification of Dr Moschos to incorporate the check valves 115 and 123 of Pan, as described with respect to claim 1 above, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 10, wherein: a first module comprises the non-rebreather, the one-way outlet valve and the one-way air inlet part (paragraph [0074], first chamber 130 including mouthpiece breath inlet port 122 (with incorporated check valve of Pan) and mouthpiece breath outlet tube 134 (with incorporated check valve of Pan)); and a second module comprises the sample delivery part and the sample collection chamber connector (figure 8a, paragraphs [0082, 0087], collection vessel housing 200 having collection vessel 300 including vessel breath tube 330).
Regarding claim 14, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 1. Dr Moschos does not disclose wherein the sample collection chamber further comprises an integrated testing module.
In a similar technical field, Pan discloses wherein the sample collection chamber further comprises an integrated testing module (figure 3, paragraphs [0066, 0068], optical reader 131/231; may be of the type which sends light signals toward the membrane 127 so that a photo-detector (not shown) may read the color of the membrane. The optical reader 131 has a display 137 to output a suitable message indicative of the presence or absence of ammonia in the sampled breath based on the color of the membrane 127 detected).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Dr Moschos such that the sample collection chamber further comprises an integrated testing module as disclosed by Pan, as such a modification would have been predictable, namely incorporating the optical reader of Pan into the collection vessel housing 200 having collection vessel 300 of Dr Moschos and incorporating the ammonia sensing membrane 127 into the collection vessel 300  of Dr Moschos such that the optical reader sends light signals toward the membrane so that a photo-detector may read the color of the membrane and output a suitable message indicative of the presence or absence of ammonia in the sampled breath based on the color of the membrane detected (Pan, paragraph [0067]).
Claims 5 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Dr Moschos in view of Pan, further in view of Sherwood, as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of Dompeling et al. (US 20100292601 A1) (herein Dompeling).
Regarding claim 5, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 1. Dr Moschos does not disclose a volumetric breath quantifier configured to measure a volume of breath delivered to the sample outlet.
In a similar technical field, Dompeling discloses a volumetric breath quantifier (paragraph [0037], flow meter 14) configured to measure a volume of breath delivered to the sample outlet (paragraph [0037], flow meter 14 used to calculate the amount of breath exhaled and hence the amount of breath collected in the gas container 6).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Dr Moschos such that the breath sampler further comprises a volumetric breath quantifier configured to measure a volume of breath delivered to the sample outlet as disclosed by Dompeling as such a modification would have been predictable, namely incorporating the flow meter of Dompeling into the mouthpiece module 100 of Dr Moschos to calculate the amount of breath exhaled and hence the amount of breath collected in the gas container (Dompeling, paragraph [0037).
Claims 6-7 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Dr Moschos in view of Pan, further in view of Sherwood, further in view of Dompeling, as applied to claim 5 above, and further in view of King-Smith (US 20170035326 A1).
Regarding claim 6, Dr Moschos, as modified to incorporate the volumetric breath quantifier, further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 5. Dr Moschos does not disclose wherein the volumetric breath quantifier is configured to separate the breath sample into at least two sub-samples.
In a similar technical field, King-Smith directed to device for capturing and concentrating volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in a sample of breath air, discloses wherein the volumetric breath quantifier is configured to separate the breath sample into at least two sub-samples (figure 6, paragraphs [0065, 0116-0118], the Exhaled Air Sampler 320 will direct a volume of exhaled air through the optional Filter 800 into the Concentrator 600; multiple Compartments 714 may hold a unique Ionic Liquid or the same Ionic Liquid as another Compartment and by mixing and matching the Ionic Liquid, different VOCs can be preferentially adsorbed by the Ionic Liquid in different Compartments; and a breath sample may be steered to one or all of the Ionic Liquid Containers at different times and by doing so, the location of a cancer within the lungs may be identified).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Dr Moschos such that the volumetric breath quantifier is configured to separate the breath sample into at least two sub-samples as disclosed by King-Smith as such a modification would have been predictable, namely incorporating the multiple compartments 714 of King-Smith into the collection vessel 300 of Dr Moschos such that different VOCs can be preferentially adsorbed by the Ionic Liquid in different compartments and such that a breath sample may be steered to one or all of the Ionic Liquid Containers at different times and by doing so, the location of a cancer within the lungs may be identified (King-Smith, paragraphs [0116-0117).
Regarding claim 7, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 6, wherein the volumetric breath sampler further comprises a closure member (paragraph [0082], cap 320 comprises a sealing mechanism in the form of a sliding lid 322 arranged to seal a vessel breath inlet 326 and a vessel exhaust outlet 328 when the lid is closed; sliding lid 322 is provided with a lip 324 operable to move the sliding lid 322 into or out of position; when the sliding lid 322 is open, the vessel breath inlet 326 and the vessel exhaust outlet 328 are accessible). Dr Moschos does not disclose wherein the volumetric breath sampler further comprises a closure member configured to selectively close the sample outlet to prevent a first sub-sample being delivered to the sample collection chamber.
In a similar technical field, King-smith discloses wherein the volumetric breath sampler further comprises a closure member (paragraph [0095], Ionic Liquid Collector 710 may have a sealing mechanism that is automatically opened and closed by the Concentrator 600) configured to selectively close the sample outlet to prevent a first sub-sample being delivered to the sample collection chamber (paragraphs [0095, 0118, 0131], the Ionic Liquid Collector 710 may have a sealing mechanism that is automatically opened and closed by the Concentrator 600; a breath sample may be steered to one or all of the Ionic Liquid Containers at different times and by doing so, the location of a cancer within the lungs may be identified; if a multi-chamber Ionic Liquid Collector 710 is used it is possible to select Ionic Liquids that are preferential to the adsorption of particular VOCs).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Dr Moschos such that the volumetric breath sampler further comprises a closure member configured to selectively close the sample outlet to prevent a first sub-sample being delivered to the sample collection chamber as disclosed by King-Smith as such a modification would have been predictable, namely incorporating the multiple Ionic Liquid containers having sealing members and the automatic opening and closing of the sealing members of King-Smith such that Ionic Liquids that are preferential to the adsorption of particular VOCs are selected and a breath sample may be steered to one or all of the Ionic Liquid Containers at different times so that the location of a cancer within the lungs may be identified (King-Smith, paragraphs [0095, 0118, 0131]).
Claims 8-9 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Dr Moschos in view of Pan, further in view of Sherwood, further in view of Dompeling, further in view of King-Smith, as applied to claim 7 above, further in view of Ahmad et al. (US 20170119280 A1) (herein Ahmad), and further in view of Akouka et al. (WO 2018071441 A1) (herein Akouka).
Regarding claim 8, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 7. Dr Moschos does not disclose wherein the volumetric breath quantifier comprises a Geneva gear configured to open the closure member when a predetermined volume of breath has entered the volumetric breath quantifier.
In a similar technical field, Ahmad directed to a breath capture device for determining the concentration of acetone in a breath sample from a user, discloses wherein the volumetric breath quantifier comprises a gear configured to open the closure member when a predetermined volume of breath has entered the volumetric breath quantifier (figures 70-71, paragraphs [0073, 0320- 0323], volume of the breath sample through the flow path is greater than 350 ml; the processor controls a solenoid valve 10015, which is manipulated through the use of an actuating mechanism; solenoid valve 10105 is attached to a linear actuator 10110 that is controlled by a dial 10115 attached to gear 10120 that can be manipulated; the rotation of the gear directly influences the pivot angle of the solenoid valve 10105, which can provide variations in between the open and closed scenario; flow sensors 10125, 10130 in both flow paths 10135, 10140 to determine when the desired vented volume has been evacuated, when to switch flow paths, and when a test has been completed).
In a similar technical field, Akouka directed to an inhaler and methods of use thereof as a device for use in administering medicament in powder form discloses a Geneva gear (figure 10, paragraph [0200], Geneva drive 1000). The instant application specification discloses a breath sampler apparatus and on page 11 lines 26-31 discloses the apparatus has a delivery port 510 facilitates a connection of a nebuliser, such as nebuliser 520, or similar breathing aide, and enables the delivery of medication such as bronchodilators, which is in the same technical field as Akouka directed to a device for use in administering medicament in powder form.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Dr Moschos such that the volumetric breath quantifier comprises a Geneva gear configured to open the closure member when a predetermined volume of breath has entered the volumetric breath quantifier as disclosed by Ahmad and Akouka as such a modification would have been predictable, namely using flow sensors in the flow paths to determine when the desired vented volume has been evacuated, when to switch flow paths, and when a test has been completed and communicating with a processor which controls the valve through a linear actuator that is controlled by a dial attached to gear, merely substituting the gear of Ahmad for the Geneva gear of Akouka, and manipulating the gear to provide variations in between the open and closed scenario (Ahmad, paragraphs [0320-0323).
Regarding claim 9, Dr Moschos further discloses the breath sampler according to claim 8. Dr Moschos does not disclose wherein the volumetric breath quantifier is positioned downstream of the outlet valve and comprises: a turnstile rotatably mounted within the breath flow pathway and comprising at least one fin configured to be rotatably displaced by a defined breath volume; a geared coupling between the turnstile and the Geneva gear; wherein the turnstile is configured to move the Geneva gear from a first position to a second position, and wherein movement of the Geneva gear from the first position to the second position is configured to open the closure member to allow a second sub-sample to be delivered to the sample collection chamber.
